overview: Thomson Reuters is a Toronto-headquartered content-and-technology company that supplies proprietary research, software and AI-enabled workflow tools to legal, tax, audit, accounting and corporate-compliance professionals, plus global news through Reuters. It reports in U.S. dollars under IFRS, is dual-listed on the TSX and Nasdaq, and is majority-controlled (~70%) by Woodbridge, the Thomson family holding company. Having exited its minority stake in LSEG and divested FindLaw and other non-core assets in 2024, the company is now a more focused "Big 3" (Legal Professionals, Corporates, Tax Audit & Accounting Professionals) plus Reuters News and a soon-to-be-deconsolidated Global Print business.

business_model.summary: Thomson Reuters sells proprietary legal, tax and compliance content bundled with AI-enabled workflow software, overwhelmingly on recurring subscription contracts (81% of 2025 revenue) with one-to-five-year terms and ~92% customer retention. Transactions revenue (12%) includes volume-based tax-filing/e-invoicing fees, software licenses and consulting; Global Print (7%, declining) sells print-format legal/tax content and third-party commercial printing, and is being 51%-sold to a KKR-advised joint venture (announced July 2026, expected to close Q4 2026). The 'Big 3' segments generated 82% of 2025 revenue and carry the highest margins and growth.

revenue_streams.name: Legal Professionals (Westlaw, Practical Law, CoCounsel Legal)
Tax, Audit & Accounting Professionals (Checkpoint, UltraTax, SafeSend)
Reuters (News Agency, Reuters.com, Reuters Events, LSEG news supply agreement)
Global Print (legal/tax print content, commercial printing)

business_model.customer_type: B2B/enterprise and government — law firms, courts, corporate legal/tax/compliance departments (including the seven largest global accounting firms), small businesses, and media organizations/professionals via Reuters; largest single customer (the LSEG news agreement) is ~5% of revenue
business_model.geographic_mix: U.S. 72% of 2025 revenues; remainder spread across U.K./EMEA, Canada, Brazil, Asia Pacific and other Latin America; 19% of revenue and 39% of operating expenses are non-USD denominated (largest FX exposure: GBP, CAD, EUR, BRL, INR)

main_competitors: Harvey AI / Casetext-style legal AI startups
competitive_position.market_position: Leading position in U.S. legal research (Westlaw) and tax/accounting workflow software (Checkpoint, UltraTax); 'Big 3' segments operate in an estimated $31 billion market management expects to grow 8-11% annually over the next five years

moat_factors.description: 1.9 billion documents, 1,500+ attorney editors producing 1.6 million editorial enhancements/year, the West Key Number System (35 million legal classifications) and KeyCite (1.4 billion citation relationships) are not readily replicable and underpin AI product accuracy/defensibility
Westlaw, Practical Law, Checkpoint and ONESOURCE are deeply embedded in daily professional workflows; 92% retention rate in 2025 and ~450,000 customers with no customer over ~5% of revenue

"Fiduciary-Grade AI" positioning (verifiable, citation-checked outputs grounded in proprietary content) differentiates CoCounsel from generic LLM tools in high-stakes, liability-sensitive professional use cases
81% recurring revenue and a largely fixed cost base support stable margins and operating leverage as revenue grows
Reuters Trust Principles and century-plus heritage support credibility, though the news segment itself is lower-margin and structurally challenged

weaknesses: AI lowers barriers to entry; well-funded, specialized, often cheaper competitors (including foundation-model vendors and open-source tools) can target narrow use cases
Customers (law firms, corporate legal/accounting departments) increasingly have the technical means to build in-house alternatives using generative AI, reducing reliance on packaged content products
Reuters segment margins declining (EBITDA margin down 320bp in 2025) amid secular pressure on traditional news distribution
Global Print in structural decline and being deconsolidated (51% sold to KKR JV)
Heavy U.S. revenue concentration (72%) ties performance to U.S. legal/accounting/corporate spending cycles

growth_drivers: Broadening adoption and monetization of CoCounsel (now CoCounsel Legal, CoCounsel for Tax & Audit) across the installed base — reported 1M+ users across 107 countries by early 2026
New AI/agentic product launches: Westlaw Advantage, Ready-to-Advise, Ready-to-Review, Audit Intelligence Analyze/Test, a planned vertical legal LLM
Tuck-in M&A to add AI-native capability (SafeSend, Additive, TimeBase, Noetica, Materia, Pagero) funded by strong balance sheet capacity
International expansion of Big 3 products into new geographic markets
Operating leverage from a largely fixed cost base as organic revenue growth (targeted ~9.5% for Big 3 in 2026) continues to outpace expense growth
Deconsolidation of low-growth, low-margin Global Print (KKR JV) expected to lift total-company organic growth rate by 60-70bp once closed
Secular tailwinds: rising regulatory/compliance complexity, accounting/legal talent shortages, and AI-driven demand for trusted, verifiable professional-grade tools

business.risk: AI-driven disruption of core legal research
business.description: Rapidly improving foundation models and AI-native entrants (e.g., Anthropic's Claude legal tools, Harvey, Casetext-style startups) could commoditize legal research/document review and let customers build in-house substitutes, eroding Westlaw's pricing power and value proposition

business.risk: Intensifying competition from agile, narrowly-focused and lower-cost entrants
business.description: Company explicitly flags increased competition from well-funded AI-focused new entrants, consumption-based pricing models undercutting subscriptions, and professional service firms (the Global 7 accounting firms) building their own competing technology
Corporate legal/tax departments and law firms could internally develop GenAI tools that substitute for packaged Thomson Reuters products, reducing demand
Traditional news agency model under pressure from digital/streaming shift; Reuters segment adjusted EBITDA margin fell 320bp in 2025

business.risk: Global Print structural decline and transaction execution risk
business.description: Ongoing revenue decline; KKR joint-venture closing (Q4 2026) carries integration/execution risk and TRI has agreed to provide a minimum-return backstop to KKR
Acquired businesses typically carry lower margins initially; failure to integrate (SafeSend, Additive, Noetica, etc.) could dilute margins or fail to deliver expected synergies

financial.description: 19% of revenue / 39% of opex in non-USD currencies (GBP, CAD, EUR, BRL, INR); USD reporting creates translation volatility

financial.risk: Rising net interest expense / leverage increase
financial.description: Net debt/adjusted EBITDA rose from 0.6x (Dec 2025) to 0.9x (June 2026) on higher commercial paper borrowings funding buybacks/return of capital; still well below the 2.5x target ceiling
Material defined benefit plans were 94% funded as of Dec 2025; future contributions depend on market/actuarial conditions
Access to debt markets and borrowing costs depend on maintaining investment-grade ratings

regulatory.description: New or enacted AI legislation could restrict how the company uses AI in products, require costly changes to offerings, or expose it to fines/penalties
Subject to antitrust laws across jurisdictions; could face claims/investigations affecting how products are offered or priced, especially given scale in legal/tax content markets

regulatory.risk: Global tax/transfer pricing and Pillar Two
regulatory.description: Operates across many tax jurisdictions; subject to audits (including an ongoing U.K. HMRC Diverted Profits Tax dispute related to divested businesses) and OECD Pillar Two minimum-tax rules

The Founders Share Company can block disposals/acquisitions involving Reuters and exercises extraordinary voting power to protect Trust Principles, which could limit strategic flexibility or deter a change of control

macro.risk: Customer spending cycles in legal/tax/accounting/corporate markets
macro.description: Demand depends on the health of the U.S. economy (72% of revenue) and secondarily the U.K., Canada, Brazil and other markets; recession, tariff/trade policy uncertainty or geopolitical shocks could slow renewals or reduce transactional volumes
Lower rates reduce interest income on cash balances (flagged as the one 2025 outlook metric missed); higher rates raise borrowing costs on debt and commercial paper
Recurring-revenue model means downturns and recoveries both show up in reported revenue with a delay, which can mask or exaggerate near-term momentum

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Management estimates the Big 3 segments address a ~$31 billion market expected to grow 8-11% annually over the next five years, driven by AI adoption, regulatory complexity and digitization of legal/tax/compliance workflows
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-to-moderate — 81% recurring subscription revenue and a largely fixed cost base make revenue historically resilient through macro downturns (slower to decline, but also slower to recover); transactional revenue (12%) and Global Print are more cyclical/secularly declining
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — net interest expense is rising as cash balances fall from buybacks/return-of-capital and commercial paper borrowings increase; net debt/EBITDA (0.9x) remains well below the 2.5x target ceiling
key_input_costs: Content/editorial labor (attorney editors, subject matter experts)

recent_developments.event: Q3 2026 earnings scheduled for November 3, 2026; company guided Q3 organic revenue growth of ~8% and adjusted EBITDA margin of ~36% (down sequentially on severance and M&A dilution, plus softer government growth)
Q2 2026 results: revenue +9% total/constant currency, +8% organic; Big 3 organic growth +10%; raised full-year 2026 outlook to ~8.0% total/organic revenue growth and 9.5-10.0% for Big 3 segments

Signed definitive agreement for a joint venture with KKR: sale of 51% of Global Print business for ~$500 million gross proceeds, retaining 49% equity interest and IP/editorial control; expected to close Q4 2026 and to be reported as discontinued operations from Q3 2026

Completed $605 million return of capital ($1.435518/share special distribution) funded by 2024 LSEG share sale proceeds, paired with a share consolidation (reverse stock split) reducing shares outstanding by ~6.5 million; Woodbridge participated

Thomson Reuters, RELX and Wolters Kluwer shares fell sharply (TRI reportedly down ~10-18% depending on source) after Anthropic launched a Claude-based legal AI plug-in aimed at contract review, compliance workflows and legal drafting, reviving investor concern about AI disintermediating legal-research incumbents even though the tool did not directly target core legal research

Announced 10% dividend increase to $2.62/share annualized (33rd consecutive year of increases, 5th consecutive 10% raise), a new up-to-$600 million NCIB buyback, the Noetica acquisition (AI-native deal-data intelligence for market professionals), and the return-of-capital/share-consolidation plan

FY2025 results: total revenue +3% (organic +7%), Big 3 organic revenue +9%, adjusted EBITDA margin 39.2% (+100bp), free cash flow $1.95 billion, met nearly all elements of updated 2025 outlook (missed only net interest expense)
Acquired Additive, a GenAI-native startup automating complex U.S. federal tax form processing (e.g., Schedule K-1) for tax preparation workflows
Acquired SafeSend, automating the 'last mile' of tax return assembly, review, e-signature and delivery

guidance.as_of: Q2 2026 Earnings (August 2026), updating FY2025 Annual Report guidance (March 2026)

items.notes: Raised in August 2026 from the original 7.5-8.0% range given in the FY2025 annual report; organic growth matches total growth
Raised from the original ~9.5% target; all other FY2026 outlook metrics reaffirmed unchanged from the May 5, 2026 outlook update
Big 3 segment adjusted EBITDA margin also guided +100bp vs 2025's 43.6%
Up from $1.95 billion actual in 2025; outlook currently still includes Global Print, to be updated at Q3 2026 release once Global Print is reported as discontinued
Up from $143 million in 2025, reflecting lower cash balances from buybacks/return of capital and higher commercial paper borrowings

items.metric: Effective tax rate on adjusted earnings

items.notes: Adjusted EBITDA margin guided ~36% for Q3, down sequentially on severance expense, M&A dilution and softer government-segment growth

items.metric: Global Print organic growth contribution post-deconsolidation
items.target: +60-70bp to total company organic growth rate; minimal impact to adjusted EBITDA margin
items.notes: Reflects expected benefit once the lower-growth Global Print segment is deconsolidated following the KKR joint-venture closing

guidance.management_commentary: Management (CEO Steve Hasker, CFO Gary Bischoping) reiterated confidence in Big 3 momentum, calling AI the 'biggest disruption... in its history' for the legal profession while positioning CoCounsel and 'Fiduciary-Grade AI' as a differentiated, trust-based response. The August 2026 guidance raise reflected broad-based strength across recurring and transactions revenue; management flagged a softer Q3 government growth rate and continued M&A-related margin dilution as near-term headwinds, alongside ongoing macro/geopolitical uncertainty as a general risk to the outlook.

bull_case: Accelerating, broad-based organic growth (raised to ~8% total / ~9.5-10% Big 3 for FY2026) with margin expansion driven by operating leverage on a largely fixed cost base

Deep, difficult-to-replicate proprietary content moat (Westlaw, KeyCite, West Key Number System) positions CoCounsel/Fiduciary-Grade AI as a trusted, defensible alternative to generic LLM legal tools rather than a casualty of them

Strong balance sheet (net debt/EBITDA well below the 2.5x ceiling) and consistent free cash flow generation (~$2.1bn guided for 2026) support continued tuck-in M&A, a 33-year dividend growth streak, and ongoing buybacks/capital returns

Portfolio simplification continues (LSEG stake and FindLaw exited 2024, Global Print 51% sold to KKR in 2026) sharpens focus on the higher-growth, higher-margin Big 3 segments and should lift reported organic growth once Global Print deconsolidates

February 2026 AI-driven selloff (on an Anthropic legal plug-in that did not even target core legal research) may represent an overreaction, per some analyst commentary describing the shares as undervalued relative to a maintained competitive moat
bear_case: Generative and agentic AI structurally threatens the economics of packaged legal/tax research: lower barriers to entry invite well-funded, narrowly focused and often cheaper competitors, and sophisticated customers (large law firms, Global 7 accounting firms, corporate legal departments) increasingly have the means to build in-house substitutes

Market has shown it will punish TRI/RELX/Wolters Kluwer sharply on any signal of AI disintermediation (the February 2026 selloff), implying elevated multiple/sentiment risk even absent fundamental deterioration

~70% Woodbridge family control and the Thomson Reuters Founders Share limit minority shareholder influence over governance, capital allocation and potential M&A/divestiture flexibility (e.g., restrictions on Reuters transactions)

Reuters and Global Print are structurally declining or being divested, meaning an increasing share of consolidated growth depends on continued Big 3/CoCounsel monetization success — any stumble in AI product execution or customer adoption has outsized impact

Heavy U.S. revenue concentration (72%) and reliance on law firm/corporate/government spending leaves the business exposed to U.S. legal-services headcount trends, government contract cancellability, and macro/trade-policy uncertainty
